content.overview: Plants raised in protected environments can experience abrupt changes in radiation, wind, temperature and water demand outdoors. Hardening is a managed transition, not simply placing plants outside on a target date.

vocabulary.definition: Gradual acclimation of transplants to outdoor environmental stress before permanent placement.
Temporary growth reduction or stress after root disturbance and environmental transition.
Period in which a transplant resumes stable root and shoot growth at the new site.

sections.title: Increase exposure gradually
sections.body: Outdoor light, wind and temperature can exceed protected-propagation conditions. Increase exposure while monitoring leaf response and water demand.

sections.title: Root condition matters at transplant
sections.body: Healthy established roots support recovery; severely stressed, root-bound or poorly rooted material is less resilient.

sections.title: Use the forecast, not only the calendar
sections.body: Delay or protect transplants when immediate frost, heat, wind or storm risk exceeds the crop's acclimation state.

workedExamples: A plant moved from low indoor PPFD directly into full midday sun can stress even when air temperature is mild.
A scheduled transplant may be postponed if a high-wind event is forecast immediately after planting.
commonMistakes: Transplanting weakly rooted material to keep a date.
content.practicalApplication: Write a multi-day acclimation plan with increasing exposure, irrigation checks and weather gates for permanent transplant.
content.summary: Successful outdoor establishment depends on gradual acclimation, healthy roots and weather-aware timing.
